query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Phase-selective recrystallization of the eutectic high-entropy alloy, applied as a tailored annealing treatment designed to fully recrystallize the softer ductile phase while retaining the hard-phase framework, will mitigate dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries and thus overcome limited room‐temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while maintaining or increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies (e.g., FCC and B2 phases) as produced by casting or rolling.
generation.intervention: Apply a single phase-selective recrystallization annealing treatment that selectively recrystallizes the soft phase while preserving the hard phase morphology.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing conditions; the treatment should be applied after a modest pre-deformation (if needed) to generate strain heterogeneity and stored energy for selective recrystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Reformed internal boundaries in which the previously un-recrystallized, incoherent ductile phase regions (sites for dislocation pile-ups) are transformed into a more homogeneous, fully recrystallized microstructure, leading to reduced local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: By eliminating weak, incoherent internal phase boundaries through selective recrystallization, the treatment reduces the accumulation of dislocations and associated stress concentrations. This minimizes microcrack nucleation while the retained hard phase framework continues to block dislocation motion and maintain high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature uniform elongation from values in untreated alloys (typically 8–14%) to approximately 35% with a concurrent maintenance or modest increase in tensile yield and ultimate strengths (targeting true stress levels near ~2 GPa).
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic alloy, with its hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure, exhibits limited ductility and premature failure due to dislocation pile-ups at its internal boundaries that trigger microcracking.
generation.boundary: The success of the intervention is contingent on achieving phase-selective recrystallization without coarsening the hard phase; thus, precise control over the annealing temperature and time is required. The approach’s efficacy may vary with composition and prior processing history.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on the exact annealing parameters and microstructural evolution during treatment; additional experimentation is needed to optimize conditions and confirm the predicted performance gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set is left untreated and the other undergoes the proposed phase-selective recrystallization annealing treatment. Characterize the microstructure using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the selective recrystallization of the soft phase and a reduction in dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation.
measurements: EBSD maps to assess grain size and recrystallized fraction of the soft phase
TEM imaging to evaluate dislocation density and distribution near phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phase-selectively recrystallized samples do not show a reduction in dislocation pile-ups (as evidenced by TEM) and fail to achieve a statistically significant increase in uniform elongation toward ~35% (or exhibit a reduction in tensile strength relative to the untreated samples) under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile

Abstract: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa.
